subject: Polity
sub_topic: Special provisions for certain states — Articles 370, 371

concepts.name: Article 370: Original Constitutional Design and Temporary Nature
key_dimensions: Placement in Part XXI ('Temporary, Transitional and Special Provisions') and its legal implications
The word 'temporary' vs. 'permanent' debate — SC interpretation in Prem Nath Koul and later cases
Instrument of Accession (IoA) as the genesis of Article 370 — its scope and limitations
Why Article 370 itself could not be amended under Article 368 — the special procedure trap

concepts.name: Mechanism of Abrogation of Article 370 (2019) and Constitutional Order
key_dimensions: Presidential Order CO 272 (2019) — how Article 367 was used to redefine 'Constituent Assembly' as 'Legislative Assembly'
Role of Governor's recommendation vs. elected government — constitutional validity question
Presidential Proclamation under Article 356 and its interaction with the abrogation process
Supreme Court verdict in In Re: Article 370 (2023) — upholding abrogation and key rationale

concepts.name: Supreme Court Judgment on Article 370 Abrogation (2023): Key Holdings
key_dimensions: Court's ruling that J&K had no 'internal sovereignty' post-accession — sovereignty trap
Validation of the use of Article 356 Proclamation to obtain concurrence of the 'Legislature'
Timeline for restoration of statehood to J&K — SC directions vs. executive action
Dissenting perspectives and minority opinions — areas of continuing legal debate

concepts.name: Bifurcation of Jammu & Kashmir into Two Union Territories (2019)
key_dimensions: J&K Reorganisation Act 2019 — J&K (with legislature) and Ladakh (without legislature) as UTs
Constitutional provision enabling downgrade from State to UT — Article 3 procedure and Parliamentary power
Whether consent of state legislature is mandatory for bifurcation — Article 3 trap ('consultation' vs. 'consent')
Comparison with other UT reorganisations (e.g., Puducherry, Delhi) — legislature vs. no-legislature distinction

concepts.name: Article 371: Overview and Distinction from Article 370
key_dimensions: Article 371 as a permanent provision vs. Article 370's temporary tag — critical difference
Scope: applies to specific states with specific protections, not blanket autonomy
Categories of protection under Article 371 — economic development, employment, law and order, land rights
Why Article 371 provisions cannot be abrogated by Presidential Order alone — requires constitutional amendment

concepts.name: Article 371A: Special Provisions for Nagaland
key_dimensions: Protected areas: Naga customary law and procedure, land and resources, ownership and transfer of land
Requirement of Nagaland Legislative Assembly's resolution before Parliament can legislate on these matters
16-Point Agreement (1960) as the genesis of Article 371A
UPSC trap: only Article 371A requires a state legislature resolution for Parliament to legislate — no other 371 provision has this exact mechanism

concepts.name: Article 371B: Special Provision for Assam
key_dimensions: Provision for a committee of Tribal Area members in the Assam Legislative Assembly
President's power to constitute and regulate this committee
Comparison with Sixth Schedule areas in Assam — overlap and distinction
Minimal scope compared to 371A — frequently tested 'least protective' contrast

concepts.name: Article 371C: Special Provision for Manipur
key_dimensions: Committee of Hill Area members in the Manipur Legislative Assembly
President's power to define 'Hill Areas' and the Governor's special responsibility
Annual report by Governor to President on administration of Hill Areas — unique reporting mechanism
Comparison with 371B (Assam) — both have tribal committees but Manipur has an additional Governor's reporting duty

concepts.name: Article 371D and 371E: Special Provisions for Andhra Pradesh (and Telangana)
key_dimensions: Presidential Orders for equitable opportunities in public employment and education for different regions
Establishment of Administrative Tribunals under 371D — jurisdiction over service matters
Article 371E: Parliament's power to establish a Central University in Andhra Pradesh — does not confer autonomy, merely enables
Post-bifurcation applicability to Telangana — whether 371D protections extend automatically

concepts.name: Article 371F: Special Provisions for Sikkim
key_dimensions: Sikkim's unique accession in 1975 — merger via 36th Constitutional Amendment
Protection of rights and interests of different sections of Sikkim's population
Continuation of pre-merger laws and their relationship with Indian law
Income tax exemption for Sikkimese — SC ruling in Assessees of Sikkim case (2023) and Article 371F(k)

concepts.name: Article 371G: Special Provision for Mizoram
key_dimensions: Protected areas: Mizo customary law and procedure, ownership and transfer of land, village administration
Similar to 371A (Nagaland) — requires Mizoram Legislative Assembly resolution for Parliament to legislate on protected matters
Mizo Accord (1986) as the political genesis
UPSC trap: 371A and 371G are the two provisions requiring state legislature resolution — students often attribute this only to 371A

concepts.name: Article 371H: Special Provision for Arunachal Pradesh
key_dimensions: Governor's special responsibility for law and order — acts in individual judgement, not on Council of Ministers' advice
This is one of the few constitutional provisions where Governor has individual discretion explicitly — UPSC trap
Comparison with other Governors' discretionary powers (Article 163) — 371H overrides CoM advice specifically on law and order
Controversy and judicial scrutiny regarding Governor's discretionary role in Arunachal Pradesh (2016 political crisis)

concepts.name: Article 371I: Special Provision for Goa
key_dimensions: Minimum strength of 30 members in the Goa Legislative Assembly — prevents dissolution into smaller house
Context: Goa's small size and political history of defections necessitating this protection
Comparison: Only provision under Article 371 that deals with the size of a state legislature
Does not protect land, culture, or employment — purely a structural/legislative protection

concepts.name: Article 371J: Special Provision for Karnataka (Hyderabad-Karnataka Region)
key_dimensions: 105th Constitutional Amendment Act (2012) — most recent addition to Article 371
Establishment of a separate development board for Hyderabad-Karnataka region (Kalyana Karnataka)
Reservation in educational institutions and state government jobs for persons from this region
UPSC trap: 371J is the newest Article 371 provision — tests awareness of constitutional amendments

concepts.name: Sixth Schedule vs. Article 371 Provisions: Overlap and Distinction
key_dimensions: Sixth Schedule creates Autonomous District Councils with legislative, judicial, and executive powers — structural autonomy
Article 371 provisions are targeted protections (land, employment, culture) without creating new governmental bodies (mostly)
States covered by both: Assam, Meghalaya, Tripura, Mizoram have Sixth Schedule AND some have Article 371 protections
UPSC trap: Sixth Schedule applies to NE states but NOT all NE states have Article 371 provisions (e.g., Meghalaya, Tripura have Sixth Schedule but no Article 371 provision)

concepts.name: Governor's Special Responsibility Under Article 371 Provisions: Comparative Analysis
key_dimensions: States where Governor has explicit special responsibility: Maharashtra & Gujarat (371), Manipur (371C), Arunachal Pradesh (371H), Sikkim (371F)
Distinction between acting in 'individual judgement' (371H) vs. acting after 'consultation' — degree of discretion varies
Whether such special responsibilities are justiciable — courts' reluctance to interfere
Contrast with Article 163: general rule is Governor acts on CoM advice; 371 provisions are constitutional exceptions

concepts.name: Article 371 (Original): Special Provisions for Maharashtra and Gujarat
key_dimensions: Development Boards for Vidarbha, Marathwada, rest of Maharashtra; and Saurashtra, Kutch, rest of Gujarat
Equitable allocation of funds for developmental expenditure and equitable opportunities in government service
Governor's special responsibility to ensure implementation — one of few cases of Governor's special role outside NE
Historical context: States Reorganisation and fear of regional neglect within newly formed linguistic states

concepts.name: Parliamentary Legislation and State Consent: Variations Across Article 371 Provisions
key_dimensions: 371A (Nagaland) and 371G (Mizoram): Parliament CANNOT legislate on protected matters without state legislature resolution
Other 371 provisions: Parliament CAN legislate; protections are implemented through Presidential Orders or Governor's role
Article 370 (old): Parliament needed 'concurrence' of state government for Union List and Concurrent List extension beyond defense, etc.
UPSC trap: Degrees of protection — 371A/371G offer strongest legislative shield; others are administrative/executive protections

concepts.name: Federalism and Special Provisions: Constitutional Philosophy
key_dimensions: Asymmetric federalism — India's model accommodates differential treatment of states based on historical, cultural, and strategic factors
Articles 370 and 371 as instruments of 'integration through accommodation' vs. uniform federalism debate
Constituent Assembly debates on special provisions — B.R. Ambedkar and Gopalaswami Ayyangar's arguments for Article 370
Post-2019 debate: whether abrogation of 370 signals a shift toward more uniform federalism and implications for 371 provisions

concepts.name: Land Rights and Transfer Protections Under Article 371 Provisions: Comparative Study
key_dimensions: 371A (Nagaland), 371G (Mizoram): Explicit protection of land ownership and transfer from non-residents
These protections coexist with Fifth and Sixth Schedule land protections — potential overlaps
Inner Line Permit (ILP) system in Nagaland, Mizoram, Manipur, Arunachal — statutory protection under Bengal Eastern Frontier Regulation 1873, NOT directly under 371
UPSC trap: ILP is often confused as an Article 371 protection — it is a separate statutory mechanism, though both serve similar purposes
